outcomeNote: The candidate removes every record from the reader's reply path and is worth nothing: -0.84% on `point1` against a zero-ceiling write control at -0.42%, and +1.24% on `bytes1`, the lane that loses two records and should have won most. The prediction it was built from -- 0.85 to 1.59 us per reply, or 17-27% of a point read -- came from an echo-isolate ladder and does not exist in the shipping path. Runtime reverted; prototype at `archive/exp-282`; both harnesses retained. The lasting contributions are the decomposition and the demonstration that the ladder can be wrong.
changedBeliefs: We believed, on claim 279.3, that roughly half of a point read's isolate hop -- about 3.1 us -- was resqlite's own per-request work, and that a decomposition would find one dominant item to attack. Both halves of that belief are now measured and both are wrong. The seven items claim 279.3 named, plus two more, sum to 78.8 ns; the largest is a `Completer.sync()` at 38.6 ns. And the hop they were subtracted from is 3.27 us today, not claim 265.1's 6.3 us, with the inline arm measured *cheaper* than exp 265's so the gap is a floor. There is no residual, so there is nothing in this family left to attack.

We believed `isolate_transport_price.dart` was, in exp 279's words, "the ruler for anything that changes what crosses the isolate boundary", and this run used it that way. It produced a confident, reproducible, five-times-hardened prediction of 17-27% that the library does not have. An echo isolate replying to a tight await loop is not the reply path, and its most faithful one-way lane (`real-rec`, 3.92 us) prices a single message above the entire 3.27 us round-trip hop it is modelling -- a self-check any future user of that harness can run in one command. We now believe a transport ladder answers relative questions inside itself and cannot price a shipping message in absolute terms.

We believed a transport question needed a transport harness. A temporary `Stopwatch` around the real worker's `eventPort.send`, twenty lines, in both worktrees, over 5,800 reads each, answered in one run what four harness variations could not: 1416.8 ns for the record and 1457.3 ns for the class. In-situ instrumentation is the first thing to reach for when a synthetic harness and an A/B disagree, not the last.

claims.text: The per-request work claim 279.3 named is worth 78.8 ns, not ~3.1 us. Measured individually and AOT: `Completer.sync()` and its resolution 38.6 ns, the `_rowHints[sql]` lookup over a full 128-entry map 9.6 ns, the worker's `setBusy` bracket (two leaf FFI calls) 5.9 ns, `RowSizeMemory.record` 5.2 ns, `materializeCells` with nothing wrapped 4.8 ns, building and destructuring the reply envelope 4.7 ns, `_dispatch`'s four-slot scan 4.7 ns, `SelectRequest` construction plus the hint stamp 2.6 ns, and `toResultSet` 2.6 ns. That is 2.4% of the hop. Claim 279.3 is refuted and no candidate in the family it opened is worth a pass.

claims.text: A point read's isolate hop is 3.27 us on current main, not claim 265.1's 6.3 us. `db.select()` of one six-column row costs 4.625 us through the pool and 1.355 us run inline on the calling isolate. The inline arm here is cheaper than exp 265's -- it skips the async prologue, the `_runtime` hop and the hint bookkeeping that exp 265's inline routing kept -- so 3.27 us is an upper bound on what the worker path adds and the gap against 6.3 us is a floor. Any calculation that still divides by 6.3 us is overstating its headroom by about a factor of two.

claims.text: An echo-isolate transport ladder reports a ~1 us penalty for a `SendPort` message containing a record that the shipping path does not have. In the ladder a record and a `List` holding identical values differ by 1.08 us (3.00 vs 1.92 us), the penalty does not scale with field count (a two-field record costs the same as a three-field one) and a second record in the same message is free; it survives pre-built vs freshly-allocated payloads, canonical vs freshly-decoded strings, a canonical vs a run-time-built schema, nesting, and a worker that burns 2.3 us before replying, at +0.85 to +1.59 us. In the library it is absent twice over: a `Stopwatch` around the real worker's `eventPort.send` reads 1416.8 ns for the record and 1457.3 ns for the class over 5,800 reads each, and the end-to-end A/B moves -0.84% where the ladder predicts -17% to -27%. The ladder's own tell is that its most faithful reply lane, 3.92 us one way, exceeds the whole 3.27 us round-trip hop it models.

claims.text: Leaving the caller parked for longer does not make a round trip cost more. With the worker burning a calibrated interval before replying, the round trip's overhead above that interval is 3.17 us at 0 us of work, 2.64 at 2.25 us, 2.71 at 4.51 us and 3.09 at 11.27 us -- flat, with no step where the caller's isolate parks. There is no wake premium hiding in the hop, and a tight ladder is not flattered by keeping its caller hot.

nextSignals: Do not open another candidate against 'the per-request half of the hop'. Claim 282.1 prices all of it at 78.8 ns and claim 282.2 halves the hop it was subtracted from. The two commands that would reopen it are `read_request_residual.dart --part=items` and `--part=e2e`; run those before believing any successor to claim 279.3.

Before trusting a number from `isolate_transport_price.dart` or `read_request_residual.dart --part=reply`, check it against the hop. If a one-way lane prices higher than the round trip it models (claim 282.3), the ladder is overstating and its absolute figures are not usable. Exp 279's claims 279.1, 279.2 and 279.4 were each confirmed end to end and are not in doubt; what is retired is using that harness alone to size a change.

When a synthetic harness and an A/B disagree by more than the A/B's control span, put a temporary `Stopwatch` in the real path in both worktrees and print it from the worker on shutdown. It took one run here and it is what the rejection rests on. Remove it in the same session -- it lives in the receipt, not in `lib/`.

`reader_reply_envelope_ab.dart` is the A/B for anything that changes the shape of what a reader replies with. Its `bytes1` lane is the most sensitive: `selectBytes` carried two records where `select` carried one, so a real reply-shape effect has to show there first.
